packets.key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the credit-card minimum-payment autopay option cut minimum-only payers by 23% at six months but did not reduce debt, and nudged autopay enrollees chose amounts only slightly above the minimum.
packets.methodology: Randomized field experiment on credit card autopay enrollment with 6-month follow-up.
packets.why_it_matters: Shows a nudge/default can move nominal enrollment behavior without changing the substantive outcome and that people anchor near the preset default level — the clearest empirical case for our support team's 'vanity enrollment' worry and for anchoring risk on a preset multiplier.
limitations: US credit-card debt context, not a savings product
effect measured on minimum-payment status, not enrollment into a savings feature
packets.relevance_reason: Closest empirical evidence that a default/nudge can lift a headline metric while leaving real behavior (and disengagement/complaint risk) largely unchanged, with anchoring on the default level.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Mandated active-choice browser screens under the EU Digital Markets Act produced large, durable shifts in usage — Firefox usage 113% higher on iOS and 12% higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, persisting 15+ months after rollout.
packets.methodology: Difference-in-differences design exploiting the staggered EU DMA-mandated rollout of browser choice screens on iOS and Android.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly answers whether forcing an active choice can produce a large, persistent shift in behavior comparable to a default — the central evidence needed to decide whether active choice captures most of the enrollment benefit without a default's disengagement risk, in an EU regulatory context.
limitations: studies default browser selection, not financial enrollment or contribution amounts
no data on whether the chosen option is actually used/engaged with beyond usage share
packets.relevance_reason: The clearest large-scale, persistent, real-world test of active choice against defaults under EU regulation, directly informing the entry-mechanism decision.
packets.title: The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act
packets.abstract: Can active choice mitigate the effects of preset defaults? We study this question using a difference-in-differences design around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions. We find large effects, with notable differences across platforms: from 15 months after the mandate onward, Firefox usage was 113 percent higher on iOS and 12 percent higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. This gap is consistent with rollout differences, as Android showed choice screens primarily on new devices, whereas iOS also showed them on existing devices.Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.
packets.tldr: Large effects are found around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions, with notable differences across platforms.

packets.key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and default auto-escalation: steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of auto-escalated employees escalate on the first date, with more opting out later.
packets.methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans accounting for job turnover, balance withdrawal on separation, and auto-escalation opt-out.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of our support team's objection: default-driven enrollment lift shrinks dramatically once realistic attrition and opt-out dynamics are included, directly bearing on whether opt-out enrollment numbers would be vanity.
limitations: retirement (401k) plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated enrollment channel differs from a self-directed app
packets.relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably deliver large, durable saving increases, with concrete effect sizes the brief explicitly asked for.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Across three experiments, including a representative sample from five European countries (n=4207), default nudges shifted risk-taking by medium-to-large effect sizes but lowered ratings of the wealth manager's advice compared to no default, especially among those who refused the default; framing of the default presentation had smaller but significant effects on allocation.
packets.methodology: Three behavioral experiments on investment-allocation defaults, including a large representative multi-country European experiment.
packets.why_it_matters: EU-based evidence that a default can carry a real reputational and perceived-manipulation cost, and that how the default is framed and presented changes its effect — directly informs whether our round-up multiplier default reads as helpful or as a dark pattern.
limitations: wealth-management/investment-allocation context rather than a savings round-up feature
advice-rating outcome, not enrollment or amount saved
packets.relevance_reason: Directly addresses the EU dark-pattern/manipulation trade-off in a consumer financial-advice setting closely analogous to ours.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation boxes raised campaign donations by over $43 million but also raised refund requests by almost $3 million, with the largest impact on smaller, less-experienced donors who apparently did not intend the recurring commitment.
packets.methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting the timing of pre-checked recurring-donation defaults across 2020 US campaign websites.
packets.why_it_matters: The closest real-world precedent for a pre-checked recurring-contribution default: it moves nominal sign-ups a lot, but a measurable share of that is unintended and gets reversed, and the effect concentrates on inexperienced/small users — precisely the disengagement and dark-pattern risk our support team is worried about.
limitations: political donations rather than a bank savings feature
refund requests are a proxy for regret, not a direct withdrawal/abandonment measure for a savings pot
packets.relevance_reason: Directly quantifies the backfire/regret cost of a pre-checked recurring commitment default, the same mechanism as auto-enrolling round-ups, with a distributional skew toward vulnerable users.
packets.title: Dark defaults: How choice architecture steers political campaign donations
packets.abstract: In the months before the 2020 U.S. election, several political campaign websites added prechecked boxes (defaults), automatically making all donations into recurring weekly contributions unless donors unchecked them. Since these changes occurred at different times for different campaigns, we use a staggered difference-in-differences design to measure the causal effects of defaults on donors' behavior. We estimate that defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million while increasing requested refunds by almost $3 million. The weekly default only impacted weekly recurring donations, and not other donations, suggesting that donors may not have intended to make weekly donations. The longer defaults were displayed, the more money campaigns raised through weekly donations. Donors did not compensate by changing the amount they donated. We found that the default had a larger impact on smaller donors and on donors who had no prior experience with defaults, causing them to start more chains and donate a larger proportion of their money through weekly recurring donations.
packets.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

packets.key_finding: Abstract-only: proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework explaining when and why default effects persist or fade downstream, driven by time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and salience of trade-offs.
packets.methodology: Conceptual taxonomy and theoretical review synthesizing the consumer default-effects literature; abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives the framework for predicting whether our round-up default will produce lasting engagement or early disengagement, and names the moderators (preferences, trade-off salience) we should measure post-launch — directly shapes what we track at 6-12 months.
limitations: abstract-only, no numeric effect sizes
general consumer behavior focus, not specific to savings/fintech products
packets.relevance_reason: The synthesis review most directly organizing the brief's central persistence/downstream question, satisfying the need for a review giving structure rather than a single estimate.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on voluntary pension saving in China, default-option nudges (along with social-norm and framing nudges) significantly reduced willingness to contribute relative to control, with default and positive-narrative nudges producing the strongest backfire, and effects varying by income, education, and gender.
packets.methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing behavioral nudges including default options on voluntary pension contribution decisions.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the internal premise that 'defaults will lift enrolment' — here a default nudge backfires and reduces willingness to contribute, with heterogeneous effects across demographic groups, exactly the counter-evidence the brief asked us to surface before committing to opt-out.
limitations: hypothetical willingness-to-contribute survey rather than real transactions
voluntary pension saving in China, a different cultural/regulatory context than an EU consumer banking app
small sample (220 participants)
packets.relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in the batch that a default can reduce rather than increase saving intentions, with explicit distributional heterogeneity.
packets.title: When Nudges Backfire: The Effect of Social Norms, Framing Effects, and Default Options on the Pension Saving Decisions in China
packets.abstract: This study investigates the impact of behavioral nudgessocial norms, loss aversion framing, default options, and positive narrativeon voluntary pension saving decisions in China. Using a randomized controlled trial administered via an online survey with 220 participants, we examine how these interventions influence both the willingness to contribute and the proportion of income allocated to pension savings. Contrary to prevailing international evidence, our results indicate that all nudges significantly reduce willingness to contribute relative to a control group, with the most substantial backfire effects observed for positive narrative and default option nudges. Furthermore, we identify important heterogeneity effects across income groups and emphasize the moderating roles of education, gender, and financial motivation. These findings underscore the critical importance of cultural, institutional, and individual factors in the design and implementation of behavioral interventions. Policy measures tailored to specific demographic segments and focused on financial education and trust-building are recommended.
packets.venue: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences

packets.key_finding: At-scale field experiments at major UK banks show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts cut unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, worth an estimated £170-240 million market-wide, though consumers still captured less than half of available savings.
packets.methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments run with UK retail banks on live customer accounts.
packets.why_it_matters: This is the closest real analogue to our decision: automatic enrollment vs. opt-in for a feature inside a consumer banking app, with real financial outcomes rather than survey intentions, and it shows defaults deliver only partial realized benefit even when they clearly move enrollment.
limitations: outcome is alert receipt/overdraft avoidance, not savings enrollment or amount saved
no explicit 6-12 month persistence breakdown given in the abstract
packets.relevance_reason: Provides a rare consumer-banking-app, at-scale field experiment on automatic enrollment vs. opt-in with quantified financial outcomes, exactly the setting the brief is missing evidence for.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: A broad review of household finance documents behavioral regularities in consumption, saving, borrowing, and payments, and surveys interventions, including choice architecture and product design, used to shape household financial outcomes.
packets.methodology: Narrative review/NBER chapter synthesizing empirical and theoretical household-finance literature; abstract-only detail.
packets.why_it_matters: Provides the broad synthesis of choice-architecture and product-design interventions in household finance the brief wants represented as a review, spanning consumer contexts beyond employer pensions.
limitations: narrative overview rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
abstract does not itself report specific default-effect magnitudes
packets.relevance_reason: Serves as the synthesis/review anchor for the choice-architecture literature across consumer financial products that the brief explicitly wants represented.
packets.title: Behavioral Household Finance
packets.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

packets.key_finding: A payment-reminder nudge in a consumer credit-card/checking platform cut late-payment fees by 14% overall but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
packets.methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil, comparing reminder vs. no-reminder groups on credit card late fees and checking-account overdraft fees.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly evidences the brief's 'who is helped and who is hurt' concern: a well-intentioned nudge in a consumer fintech setting produced a subgroup that was made worse off, which is exactly the risk the support team raises about defaulting everyone into round-up savings — some users may be net harmed even as average enrolment or engagement rises.
limitations: studies reminder nudges, not enrolment defaults or preset contribution levels
credit card/overdraft fees rather than savings enrolment or amounts
Brazilian market, not EU consumer-protection context
abstract gives no 6-12 month persistence data
packets.relevance_reason: Strong consumer-fintech RCT evidence of heterogeneous nudge effects, directly informing the distributional/manipulation-risk question the brief flags as essential before building.
packets.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
packets.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

alternates.key_finding: Field experiments show 'enhanced active choice', active choice framed to highlight losses from the non-preferred option, motivates behavior change and is proposed as a substitute for automatic enrollment where opt-out defaults are infeasible or ethically fraught.
alternates.methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and an enhanced active choice variant against standard choice conditions.
alternates.why_it_matters: The most directly relevant prior work on the active-choice entry design: shows active choice can motivate behavior change without a default, and offers an 'enhanced' variant adaptable to the round-up onboarding flow.
limitations: primarily tested in medication-adherence/health settings, not financial products
abstract does not report enrollment or persistence effect sizes for the financial analogy it discusses
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly informs the entry-mechanism decision by testing active choice as an alternative to opt-out defaults, the core comparison the brief asks about.
alternates.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
alternates.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: Australians rated financial nudges positively overall, preferring System 2 (reflective) framing and savings-framed interventions, with demographic variation in approval.
alternates.methodology: Pre-registered online survey experiment, 2,100 Australians, 36 hypothetical financial-intervention vignettes varying transparency, framing, and System 1/2 targeting.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly tests when a financial nudge is perceived as manipulative versus acceptable, informing how the round-up entry/level choice should be framed to avoid a dark-pattern reputational risk.
limitations: hypothetical vignettes, not actual product behavior
Australian sample, not EU
measures stated approval, not enrollment or savings outcomes
alternates.relevance_reason: Provides direct evidence on the manipulation-perception question central to the EU dark-pattern risk the brief raises.
alternates.title: Do people like financial nudges?
alternates.abstract: Abstract Do people like financial nudges? To answer that question we conducted a pre-registered survey presenting people with 36 hypothetical scenarios describing financial interventions. We varied levels of transparency (i.e., explaining how the interventions worked), framing (interventions framed in terms of spending, or saving), and ‘System’ (interventions could target either System 1 or System 2). Participants were a random sample of 2,100 people drawn from a representative Australian population. All financial interventions were tested across six dependent variables: approval, benefit, ethics, manipulation, the likelihood of use, as well as the likelihood of use if the intervention were to be proposed by a bank. Results indicate that people generally approve of financial interventions, rating them as neutral to positive across all dependent variables (except for manipulation, which was reverse coded). We find effects of framing and System. People have strong and significant preferences for System 2 interventions, and interventions framed in terms of savings. Transparency was not found to have a significant impact on how people rate financial interventions. Financial interventions continue to be rated positive, regardless of the messenger. Looking at demographics, we find that participants who were female, younger, living in metro areas and earning higher incomes were most likely to favor financial interventions, and this effect is especially strong for those aged under 45. We discuss the implications for these results as applied to the financial sector.

alternates.key_finding: Maps EU dark-pattern law onto a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations, arguing EU regulation of pre-selected defaults is fundamentally about protecting consumer autonomy rather than banning defaults outright.
alternates.methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis and taxonomy-building; abstract-only.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives the EU legal framework for distinguishing a helpful pre-selected default from a manipulative one, directly bearing on whether opt-out entry into round-up savings is defensible or a reputational/regulatory risk.
limitations: legal/doctrinal rather than empirical, no effect sizes
not specific to financial savings products
alternates.relevance_reason: Only paper in the batch that directly addresses when a default is a regulatorily-flagged dark pattern in the EU, which the brief names as a reputational risk.
alternates.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
alternates.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.

alternates.key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, each $1 spent on savings subsidies raised total saving by only 1 cent, while automatic employer contributions substantially raised wealth accumulation because roughly 85% of people are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies.
alternates.methodology: Large-scale administrative panel analysis of the Danish population's retirement and taxable savings accounts.
alternates.why_it_matters: The clearest large-scale evidence that defaults change real accumulated savings, not just nominal enrollment, and that the people defaults most affect are the least financially sophisticated, central to the 'who is helped, who is hurt' question, though in an employer/government retirement setting rather than a liquid consumer product.
limitations: Danish employer- and government-administered retirement/taxable accounts, not a self-directed consumer banking app
locked, non-liquid retirement savings vehicles
alternates.relevance_reason: The strongest available evidence on whether defaults move real savings amounts and on who is passive versus active, even though the setting is employer-mediated retirement accounts.
alternates.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
alternates.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.

alternates.key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85%, but about 80% of enrollees initially stuck with the low default contribution rate and conservative default fund, and half still did after three years.
alternates.methodology: Multi-year administrative data analysis across three large US firms with automatic 401(k) enrollment.
alternates.why_it_matters: The canonical demonstration that defaults raise enrollment but also anchor people at the pre-set level for years, the exact anchoring risk the round-up multiplier default decision needs to guard against.
limitations: employer-administered retirement plan, not a consumer banking app
published 2001, predates current app/liquidity/regulatory context
alternates.relevance_reason: Foundational evidence for the anchoring-on-preset-levels concern, though set in an employer retirement context the brief says doesn't transfer directly.
alternates.title: For Better or For Worse: Default Effects and 401(k) Savings Behavior
alternates.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan. Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation. We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so. As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle. We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund). Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund. The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward. While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation. In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average. However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.
